abstract.title: ABSTRACT
abstract.p: Lung vasculature arises from both pulmonary and systemic (bronchial) circulations. Remodeling and structural changes in lung vasculature have been recognized in end‐stage fibrotic lung diseases such as idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) but have not been well characterized. The vasculature that expands and supplies lung cancers is better described, with the recent recognition that systemic bronchial circulation expands to be the main blood supply to primary lung tumors. Here, we use publicly available single‐cell RNA‐sequencing (scRNA‐seq) data to compare vascular endothelial cell (EC) populations in multiple progressive interstitial lung diseases (ILD) and non‐small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) to identify common and distinct features. Lung tissue specimens were collected from healthy lung tissue (n = 59), ILD (n = 97), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (n = 22), and NSCLC (n = 8). We identify two subtypes of expanded EC populations in both ILD and NSCLC, “Bronch‐1” and “Bronch‐2”, expressing transcripts associated with venules and angiogenic tip/stalk cells, respectively. Relative to pulmonary capillary and arterial ECs, bronchial ECs show low expression of transcripts associated with vascular barrier integrity. The pan‐bronchial EC marker COL15A1 showed positive staining in lung parenchyma from patients with IPF, SSc‐ILD, and NSCLC, whereas positive staining was limited to subpleural and peri‐bronchial regions in non‐fibrotic controls. In conclusion, expansion of a subset of ECs expressing markers of the bronchial circulation is one of the most pronounced changes in vascular cell composition across multiple ILDs and NSCLC. These data support additional studies to determine the role of the bronchial vasculature in ILD progression.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Many interstitial lung diseases (ILD) such as idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) are characterized by progressive fibrosis of distal lung parenchyma that ultimately leads to respiratory failure and death. The current paradigm for fibrogenesis involves a combination of genetic predisposition and repeated epithelial injury resulting in progressive fibrotic replacement of normal lung units. These changes occur in the setting of pathologic processes involving multiple cell types, including epithelial cell dysfunction [1, 2], increased vascular permeability [3], recruitment of inflammatory myeloid populations [4, 5, 6], and expansion of fibroblasts into airspaces, where they persist in activated phenotypes [7]. Single‐cell RNA‐sequencing (scRNA‐seq) performed on explanted fibrotic distal lung parenchyma from IPF and other progressive pulmonary fibrosis (PPF) patients [4, 8, 9, 10] has contributed to the discovery of novel cell types that may be involved in ILD pathophysiology. For example, an aberrant epithelial population that persists in a transitional state between alveolar type 2 (AT2) and AT1 differentiation, as well as a population of SFTPB+ SFTPC+ SCGB3A2+ “AT0” cells, are both highly enriched in fibrotic tissue [4, 8, 11]. Similar experimental approaches led to the discovery of a unique CTHRC1‐expressing fibroblast population that promotes fibrosis in IPF and systemic sclerosis‐associated ILD (SSc‐ILD) [12, 13].

Endothelial cells are critical for lung function, with a central role in gas exchange within the pulmonary circulation and transport of systemic blood in the bronchial circulation. The alveolar‐capillary unit is highly specialized, with thin, elongated capillary endothelial cells (ECs) termed “aerocytes” or “aCap” intimately associated with alveolar epithelium [14, 15, 16, 17]. Epithelial damage likely impacts adjacent endothelium, and these cell populations likely need to repair in concert to regenerate functional alveoli [14, 18]. The co‐interdependence of these cells is highlighted by the observation that aCap development requires AT1 cell‐derived Vegfa [14], and genetic variants in FOXF1 that impair pulmonary capillary development result in impaired AT1 differentiation and epithelial simplification [19].

Endothelial dysfunction, including the hallmark feature of increased vascular permeability, has been identified in patients with IPF [20] by assessment of the protein permeability index (the ratio of BALF to plasma protein) [21] and, more recently, using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) [3, 20]. Vascular changes in fibrotic lungs have also been documented in observational studies including post‐mortem angiography, demonstrating increased broncho‐pulmonary anastomoses suggestive of vascular expansion [22]. More recently, computed tomography imaging identified parameters such as vessel volume, density, and heterogeneity as correlates with lung function decline and mortality risk [23, 24]. Finally, preclinical models have linked endothelial barrier dysregulation to fibrosis development [25, 26, 27], collectively raising the possibility that vasculature can potentiate lung fibrosis.

While there is mounting evidence of significant changes in lung endothelium co‐occurring with fibrosis, investigations have largely focused on epithelial dysfunction, fibroblast activity and collagen deposition, which has led to FDA approval of pirfenidone and nintedanib for IPF [28, 29] as well as multiple agents at various stages of preclinical and clinical development targeting fibrotic pathways [30, 31, 32, 33, 34, 35] and immune cells [36, 37, 38]. However, both current and emerging antifibrotic therapies have vasoactive properties including effects on vessel tone, permeability, angiogenesis, as well as hemostasis [39]. While endothelial targets may offer complementary therapeutic avenues, their contribution to IPF remains understudied. Notably, a therapy capable of halting or reversing disease progression has not been identified.

scRNA‐seq studies of tissue from IPF patients have reported decreased density of alveolar capillaries and expansion of an EC population expressing COL15A1 as well as venous endothelium markers (e.g., ACKR1) [4, 40]. Subsequent investigation revealed that in healthy lung tissue COL15A1+ ECs localize to subpleural and peri‐bronchial regions and are presumably part of the systemic (i.e. non‐pulmonary) circulation [16]. More recently, spatial transcriptomic analyses demonstrated that the density of COL15A1+ ECs correlates with the degree of structural remodeling in fibrotic lungs [41]. The functional significance of these expanded ECs is not known, and it is not clear if the COL15A1+ EC population expands in contexts other than IPF.

While much remains unknown about expansion of pulmonary vascular populations in ILD, the role of expanded pulmonary vasculature has been most studied in the context of lung cancer [42, 43, 44, 45]. Efforts have been made to both understand and target endothelium in lung cancers in the modern era, beginning with antiangiogenic drug design around 1971 [46] to the paradigm‐shifting concept of normalization of tumor vasculature around 2005 [42, 43, 44, 45]. More recently, unbiased transcriptomic insights from scRNA‐seq identified expansion of COL15A1+ systemic ECs in lung carcinoid tumors [47] as well as adenocarcinoma [48, 49]. A large, endothelium‐focused survey of non‐small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) enriched for ECs before single‐cell sequencing and identified multiple tumor‐enriched EC subtypes [50]. A relationship between these EC subtypes and the COL15A1+ ECs identified in ILD has not been established by integrative analysis. It is possible that features of COL15A1+ ECs identified in one disease context may inform others; for example, a transcriptomic similarity between NSCLC “tip cells” and the COL15A1+ ECs in ILD may imply angiogenic potential for the latter. Furthermore, if ectopic ECs in ILD and NSCLC are transcriptomically similar, this may imply that COL15A1+ systemic ECs expand in both contexts.

Here, we integrate scRNA‐seq data to characterize EC populations in multiple forms of ILD [10, 12, 51] as well as NSCLC [50]. We report expansion of two COL15A1‐expressing bronchial EC populations, termed Bronch‐1 and Bronch‐2, which may expand from systemic (non‐pulmonary) vasculature in IPF, SSc‐ILD, and adenocarcinoma. Bronch‐2 shared features with tumor‐associated ECs called “tip cells” and “immature ECs”, suggesting that Bronch‐2 ECs resemble an angiogenic population. These findings may feed into therapeutic designs that include endothelium as an actionable component in ILD.

sec.title: Patients with IPF and PPF Show Similar Changes In Lung Endothelial Cell Composition
sec.p: For insight into the cellular composition of IPF and PPF, we performed integration and semi‐supervised clustering of 636,387 cells from control donors (n = 59) as well as patients with IPF (n = 71), SSc‐ILD (n = 11), COPD (n = 22), or a different form of progressive ILD (n = 15) using publicly available scRNA‐seq data (Figure 1A) and previously described markers of cell types (Supplemental Table S1) [10, 12, 51]. COPD samples were included as a non‐ILD comparator. Differential expression analysis (Supplemental Table S2, S3) revealed that the resultant clusters expressed markers of previously identified epithelial, fibroblast, vascular, myeloid, and lymphoid cell types (Figure S1) [4, 8, 15]. Expression of the marker COL15A1 was highest in the bronchial EC population and was not detected in most other cell types (Figure S2). Cells from the majority of nonimmune clusters were apparent in each integrated data set (Figure S3).

caption.p: Ectopic COL15A1+ “bronchial” ECs are a feature of IPF and PPF. (A) Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) embedding of 636,387 cells from explanted lung tissue from 178 donors. Annotations from semi‐supervised clustering are shown. Vascular endothelial cells (vEC) are encircled. (B) The proportion of each cell type as a fraction of all cells was computed for each IPF, SSc‐ILD, COPD, and control sample using propeller [52]; the log2‐transformed mean proportion ratio of IPF (left), SSc‐ILD (middle) and COPD (right) relative to control is shown. Light blue arrows indicate the VE_Bronch cluster. Red points indicate FDR (Benjamini‐Hochberg p‐value) < 0.001. (C) Boxplots of the proportion of indicated cell types; data points represent samples. (D) IHC staining for COL15A1 (brown) in Control (Normal), IPF, PPF (SSc‐ILD), and COPD specimens. Low‐magnification images (top) and high‐magnification images of boxed fields (bottom) are shown. Images are representative of observations from 5 patients in each ILD group. Scale bar 200 μm. (E) Quantification of COL15A1 IHC staining area (left) and COL15A1+ vessel number (right); data points represent samples (Control n = 4; IPF n = 5; SSc‐ILD n = 5). One‐way ANOVA. ∗p < 0.05; ∗∗p < 0.005; ****p < 0.0001.

sec.p: To identify changes in endothelial composition in ILD in the context of all identified cell types, we computed the cellular composition of each sample and compared IPF, SSc, and COPD samples against control samples (Figure 1B). In IPF samples, cell populations most increased in proportion included basal and aberrant basaloid cells, SPP1+ macrophages, bronchial ECs (VE_bronch), myofibroblasts, and vascular smooth muscle cells. In SSc‐ILD samples, the most significantly increased population was bronchial ECs (VE_bronch), followed by vascular smooth muscle cells, pericytes, SPP1+ macrophages, and myofibroblasts (Figure 1B). The frequency of bronchial ECs was also increased in IPAF, CTD‐ILD, and idiopathic NSIP (I‐NSIP) samples relative to controls. In contrast, COPD samples showed a similar proportion of bronchial ECs relative to controls and showed higher proportions of mesothelial and immune cell types (e.g., dendritic cells, B cells) (Figure 1B,C). The frequencies of both AT1 and AT2 cells were reduced in IPF and SSc‐ILD (Figure 1B,C). These data expand upon previous observations of cellular composition in lungs of ILD and COPD patients and suggest that COL15A1+ bronchial EC expansion may be a conserved feature of progressive pulmonary fibrotic diseases. Additionally, the normal numbers of COL15A1+ bronchial EC in COPD patients suggest increased COL15A1+ ECs in ILD are not a general feature of alveolar destruction with capillary dropout, but is an active expansion of this cell population in ILD.

To localize bronchial ECs, we performed IHC for COL15A1 in lung sections from non‐ILD (COPD) and ILD (IPF, SSc‐ILD) patients. Co‐immunostaining for the endothelial markers ERG or CD31 with COL15A1 showed that COL15A1+ structures are endothelial (Figure S4). In non‐ILD “normal” specimens, strong COL15A1 staining was limited to peribronchiolar and subpleural regions, as shown previously [16], with COL15A1+ vascular structures appearing capillary or venule‐like and lacking a definable tunica media (Figure 1D). Other structures of the distal lung parenchyma, including alveoli, did not show evidence of COL15A1 expression. In stark contrast, in sections from patients with IPF and SSc‐ILD, COL15A1+ structures were widespread throughout regions of patchy interstitial fibrosis and significantly enriched in IPF and SSc‐ILD lung sections (Figure 1D,E). The central areas of fibroblastic foci lacked COL15A1+ structures, though COL15A1+ structures were noted to cluster around the periphery of fibroblastic foci (Figure 1D). The COL15A1+ structures encircled the honeycomb cyst areas of fibrotic lung and seem to localize near areas of dense fibrosis. Notably, the COL15A1+ structures extended further outside the smooth muscle layer surrounding the airways than in normal tissue. This pattern implies the absence of a regulatory mechanism responsible for maintaining bronchial vessels within the airway smooth muscle layer. Collectively, these data suggest that COL15A1+ bronchial EC expansion throughout distal lung parenchyma is a feature of SSc‐ILD and IPF.

sec.title: Identification of Two COL15A1+ “Bronchial” EC Subtypes in IPF, PPF, and NSCLC
sec.p: Given that lung cancer is also associated with active expansion of surrounding vascular populations, we sought to interrogate endothelial cells derived from lung cancer patients and compare them to the vascular changes identified in IPF subjects. We analyzed publicly available scRNA‐seq data of FACS‐sorted endothelial cells from patients with NSCLC (n = 8) that includes tumor endothelial cells (TEC) and adjacent normal endothelial cells (NEC) [50]. We examined expression of previously identified gCap, aCap, venous, arterial, and bronchial EC markers in endothelial populations annotated by the authors of the study (Figure S5). We identified expression of bronchial EC markers PLVAP and COL15A1 in the populations termed “immature”, “tip cell”, and “activated postcapillary venule (pcv)” by the study authors [50]. Each of these populations was enriched in the tumor‐adjacent TEC relative to NEC. Notably, “tip cells” are best known for their association with neovascularization via sprouting angiogenesis [50, 53], and a population termed “immature” (stalk) was most similar to “tip cells” [50] (Figure S5). In most models of sprouting angiogenesis, tip and stalk ECs are dynamically regulated in the microenvironment of the angiogenic front, continuously competing for the leading tip position through organotypic signaling pathways (e.g. VEGF, NOTCH, WNT), while coordinating sprout formation, proliferation, and vessel stabilization [54]. Together, these data suggest an angiogenic potential of bronchial ECs.

For insight into endothelial heterogeneity in both ILD and NSCLC, we extracted and integrated ECs from ILD and NSCLC datasets using unsupervised clustering, revealing previously described EC populations [55] termed gCap (CD36+ ), aCap (EDNRB+ ), arterial (DKK2+ ), venous (PTGSD+ ; ACKR1+), and two COL15A1+ bronchial EC populations which we designated Bronch‐1 and Bronch‐2 (Figure 2A). We identified these EC populations in all of the normal and pathologic datasets, including control, COPD, NEC, IPF, SSc and TEC (Figure 2B). Transcripts enriched in each EC population were identified for each of the six EC populations identified through our clustering analysis (Figure 2C, see also Supplemental Table S4). An expanded list of genes represented in each of the EC subclusters is shown in a heatmap in Figure 2D. These EC populations were identified across integrated datasets (Figure S6).

caption.p: Identification of two expanded COL15A1+ “bronchial” EC subtypes in IPF, PPF, and NSCLC through transcriptional profiling. (A) Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) plot of ECs integrated across multiple datasets (see Materials and Methods). (B) UMAP with cells colored according to indicated disease. (C) UMAP plots with cells color‐coded to indicate expression of indicated genes. (D) Expression heatmap of selected transcripts that distinguish EC subtypes. (E) Boxplots of the proportion of indicated EC subtypes among the 6 predominant vascular EC types (Artery, Bronch‐2, Bronch‐1, Venous, gCap, aCap). Each data point is a sample. (F) Stacked bar plot (left) and table (right) depicting the mean proportion of EC subtypes for indicated patient populations.

sec.p: Transcripts enriched in each cluster were identified by differential expression analysis (Supplemental Table S4). Bronch‐1 cells share features with venous ECs (e.g. expression of ACKR1, VCAM1, SELE) (Figure 2C,D) and likely represent the population termed “systemic venous EC” by others [16, 40]. Bronch‐2 ECs and proliferating ECs (EC‐prolif; TOP2A+ ) expressed genes that are associated with endothelial tip cells, including PGF, ANGPTL2, LOX [50, 56] (Figure 2C,D). In contrast to arterial and alveolar capillary populations, Bronch‐1 and Bronch‐2 ECs showed decreased expression of genes that promote vascular barrier integrity, including CDH5, CLDN5, S1PR1, and SMAD6 [57, 58] and increased expression of PLVAP, a marker of high‐permeability vasculature in the central nervous system [59, 60] which has been reported to facilitate leukocyte trafficking [61] (Figure 2C,D). Several genes that are highly enriched in NSCLC “immature” ECs and/or “tip cells” [50] were enriched in both Bronch‐1 and Bronch‐2, including APOLD1, LAMC1, ANGPT2, INSR, LAMB1, VIM, COL18A1, ACTG1, MARCKSL1, PLPP1, MGLL, and PLVAP (Figure 2C,D). Among vascular ECs, the proportion of Bronch‐1 and Bronch‐2 cells was increased across multiple ILDs, including IPF, SSc, I‐NSIP, IPAF, CTD‐ILD, and cHP, as well as in TECs (Figures 2B, 2E,F). We noted that the average ratio of the proportion of Bronch‐1:Bronch‐2 ECs was ~4:1 in Controls, whereas in IPF, SSc, and TECs the ratio was reduced to ~3:1 or lower (Figure 2F, Figure S7). Similar to observed alveolar epithelial cell loss in ILD, we and others [4] identify alveolar capillary reduction in ILD, more notably for the aCap population (Figure 2E,F).

sec.title: Endothelial Cell Types Enriched in Lung Adenocarcinoma Resemble COL15A1+ Bronch‐1 and Bronch‐2 ECS
sec.p: We next considered only the NEC and TEC cells in NSCLC subtypes [50] and determined the cellular composition for each sample according to cluster designations from our integrated analysis (Figure 2). As observed in ILD lung tissue, the proportion of Bronch‐1 and Bronch‐2 ECs was increased in NSCLC, most notably adenocarcinoma, whereas aCap ECs were decreased (Figure 3A). We separated the NEC and TEC cells according to their cluster designation from the original study (“Goveia et al. annotations”) [50] and computed the proportional composition of each using the designations from our integrated analysis, revealing that “immature” and “tip cells” were primarily in the Bronch‐2 cluster, whereas activated postcapillary venule (pcv) cells were predominantly Bronch‐1 ECs (Figure 3B). Cells annotated as arterial or belonging to alveolar capillaries were aligned between the two sets of cluster annotations.

caption.p: COL15A1+ Bronch‐2 ECs resemble tip cells in lung adenocarcinoma tissue. (A) Proportion of Artery, Bronch‐2, Bronch‐1, Venous, gCap, aCap, and EC‐prolif in NSCLC subtypes (adenocarcinoma, squamous cell, large cell). Each data point represents a patient. (B) (Top) UMAP plots with cells color‐coded according to clustering designation from the integrated analysis (Figure 1) or cluster designation by Goveia et al. [50]. (Bottom) Proportion of EC clusters (Artery, Bronch‐2, Bronch‐1, Venous, gCap, aCap, EC‐prolif) that comprise EC subtypes annotated by Goveia et al. [50] (immature, tip cell, postcapillary, activated postcapillary venule (pcv), arteries, cap activated, cap alveolar type I, cap alveolar type II). (C) IHC for COL15A1 and Mason trichrome staining (collagen) of adenocarcinoma specimens. Scale bar 200 μm.

sec.p: Immunostaining for the pan‐bronchial marker COL15A1 revealed extensive positive staining in vascular structures of adenocarcinoma samples, including in regions with associated fibrosis (Figure 3C). Intriguingly, COL15A1+ staining was also observed in alveolar capillaries in areas of lepidic tumor spread (Figure S8), suggesting that COL15A1+ EC could potentially also arise through transformation of existing capillary populations. Review of scRNAseq data from both ILD and NSCLC tissue again confirmed an enrichment of COL15A1 expression within the Bronch‐1 and Bronch‐2 ECs (Figures 2A, 2C,D), and we did not identify a COL15A1+ group of cells that may represent a “transitional” EC subtype. The origin of these expanded ECs remains uncertain, however these data leave open the possibility that expansion of COL15A1+ EC may arise through a combination of migration and/or angiogenesis of the bronchial circulation and transformation of capillary populations in both NSCLC and ILD.

sec.title: Characterization of Two COL15A1+ Bronchial EC Subtypes
sec.p: As noted above, Bronch‐2 ECs are distinguished from Bronch‐1 ECs by expression of genes associated with promotion of sprouting angiogenesis, including KDR/VEGFR2 [54, 62, 63], NOTCH4 [64], CD34 [65, 66], PGF [50], CTNNB1 [67, 68], SOX18 [69, 70, 71], MMP2 [72, 73], APOLD1 [74], LOX [56, 75, 76], MEF2C [77], INSR [62, 63], among others (Figure 4A). We noted that several transcripts enriched in Bronch‐2 ECs were also enriched in arterial ECs, including PLPP1, CD9, CXCL12, NOTCH4, RBP7, and SOX18 (Figure 4A). Bronch‐1 ECs, in contrast, are enriched with markers of venules/postcapillary venules (e.g., ACKR1, SELE) [15, 16] (Figure 4A). Immunofluorescence co‐staining for ACKR1 and COL15A1 in IPF lung tissue revealed both double positive Bronch‐1 ECs (COL15A1+; ACKR1+ ) and single positive Bronch‐2 ECs (COL15A1+; ACKR1‐) (Figure 4B), demonstrating existence of both subclusters of bronchial ECs in the fibrotic lung. Immunofluorescence co‐staining for COL15A1 and PGF, which was reported as a tip cell marker in NSCLC [50] and is enriched in Bronch‐2 ECs (Figure 4A), revealed COL15A1+; PGF+ cells in the fibrotic lung (Figure 4C). Of note, the top 40 Bronch‐2 markers were expressed in Bronch‐2 cells from patients with lung tumors as well as in ILD (IPF, SSc) patients, indicating common features of Bronch‐2 cells, including markers of angiogenesis, across these pathologies (Figure S9).

caption.p: Immunofluorescence validation of two COL15A1+ bronchial EC subtypes at the protein level. (A) Expression dotplot for indicated genes with enrichment in Bronch‐1 ECs, Bronch‐2 ECs, or both. (B) Immunofluorescence staining of lung parenchyma from patients with IPF for COL15A1 and ACKR1 reveals ACKR1+ ; COL15A1+ (stars) and ACKR1‐; COL15A1+ (arrows) cells. (C) Immunofluorescence staining of lung parenchyma from patients with IPF for COL15A1 and PGF reveals PGF+ ; COL15A1+ cells. Scale bar 50μm.

sec.title: COL15A1+ Vascular Structures in Early‐Stage IPF May Associate With Poorer Outcomes
sec.p: The vast majority of ILD tissue samples available for analysis are derived from explants representing end‐stage disease. We sought to evaluate whether COL15A1+ vascular structures appear earlier in the course of the disease process and therefore may be involved in disease pathogenesis or carry prognostic implications. We analyzed tissue specimens obtained in a previous study [78] which screened a population with family history of IPF to identify asymptomatic subjects with preclinical ILD. Biopsy lungs tissue from 6 subjects were obtained and stained for COL15A1. Higher levels of COL15A1 vascular staining were observed in sections of patients that went on to experience severe disease and death (Figure 5A), whereas fewer vascular COL15A1+ structures were identified in patients with milder disease (Figure 5B,D).

caption.p: COL15A1+ vascular structures in early‐stage IPF associate with poorer outcomes. IHC staining was performed on surgical lung biopsies from asymptomatic family members of IPF patients who had early disease on chest imaging. (A) IHC for COL15A1 and Mason trichrome staining (collagen) on an asymptomatic ILD patient with rapid progression of disease. (B) IHC for COL15A1 and Mason trichrome staining (collagen) on an asymptomatic ILD patient with slow progression of disease. (C) Table relating the density of COL15A1 immunostaining on tissue biopsy and pace of disease progression for 7 donors. Scale bar 200 μm. (D) Quantification of COL15A1 IHC staining area (top) and COL15A1+ vessel number (bottom) from samples in (C), “progression to severe disease” defined as patients who developed PF and died within 10 years of biopsy, “progression to mild disease” defined as patients who developed mild PF or had slow decline in PFTs; data points represent samples.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: IPF is the prototypic progressive interstitial lung disease (ILD), but many other forms of ILD have been found to be progressive and lead to severe morbidity and mortality. Different forms of ILD are believed to stem from unique combinations of factors, such as risk alleles [79, 80, 81, 82, 83], autoantibody repertoires [38, 84, 85, 86, 87, 88, 89], and environmental exposures [90]. Despite these differences, scRNA‐seq data [5, 51, 91] are revealing common cellular features among end‐stage fibrotic lung tissue. While angiogenesis is a core aspect of scar formation in general [92], histologic studies of pan‐endothelial markers in ILD have led to conflicting observations of endothelial dropout and expansion [93, 94, 95, 96, 97]. These conflicting observations can be reconciled if we consider concomitant alveolar capillary dropout with systemic bronchial (COL15A1+ ) vascular expansion [4, 40]. Indeed, pioneering work from Dame Margaret Turner‐Warwick in 1963 [22] demonstrated expansion of bronchial vasculature in fibrotic human lungs, and it has long been appreciated that vessels stemming from bronchial arteries can supply human lung tumors [98, 99, 100, 101]. Here, we provide transcriptomic and histologic evidence that bronchial EC expansion is a general feature of end‐stage progressive pulmonary fibrotic diseases and is identifiable in NSCLC tissue. In addition, we describe two populations of bronchial ECs that occur in stereotyped ratios, with the smaller bronchial population expressing features associated with sprouting angiogenesis.

Bronchial ECs have been reported to be enriched to a similar extent in the lungs of patients with end‐stage IPF and patients who died from severe COVID‐19 [40], supporting the hypothesis that bronchial EC expansion may be a generalizable feature of end‐stage fibrotic lung disease. The disease course for these COVID‐19 patients ranged from ~15‐50 days [40], suggesting that bronchial EC expansion can occur rapidly in tandem with tissue damage. The study [40] used single‐nucleus RNA‐seq and identified two bronchial EC populations, termed “systemic venous” (POSTN+; SPRY1+; ZNF385D+; COL15A1+) and “systemic capillary” (PLVAP+; INSR+; COL15A1+), consistent with expression profiles for Bronch‐1 and Bronch‐2 ECs described here. In addition, “systemic venous” ECs were identified more frequently than “systemic capillary” ECs [40], consistent with our observation that the ratio of Bronch‐1: Bronch‐2 is ~2.8. Intussusceptive angiogenesis has been documented in lungs of patients who died from COVID‐19, wherein histologic features of both intussusceptive and sprouting angiogenesis correlated with days in hospital [102]. While our analysis did not identify an EC population in a “transitional” state between alveolar capillary and bronchial, it is possible that a portion of bronchial ECs, as defined by transcriptome signature, are generated from pre‐existing pulmonary capillaries. Using multiplex IF staining of early‐stage IPF, Lang et al. (2023) [103] identified ECs in thickened alveolar septa with ectopic expression of PLVAP and VWA1 (bronchial EC markers) and undetectable expression of periaxin (PRX; alveolar capillary marker), which suggests a phenotypic change of alveoli‐associated endothelial cells towards a bronchial EC phenotype. These observations are consistent with our identification of COL15A1+ capillaries in septa with lepidic tumor in NSCLC biopsies. However, murine models of lung fibrosis have not revealed an ectopic EC population analogous to bronchial ECs, but instead demonstrated a bleomycin‐induced gCap phenotype switch to “activated” or “undifferentiated” states [104]. Murine models may also be limited in their ability to answer these questions due to the notable lack of bronchial circulation in mouse lungs. Longitudinal analysis of human ILD and nonhuman ILD models that track Bronch‐1, Bronch‐2, and alveolar capillary populations will be needed to discern the lineage of expanded bronchial vasculature in lung fibrosis.

It is not well understood if endothelial changes in ILD are solely a response to the fibrotic process or also contribute to disease progression. The development of normal alveolar epithelium depends on the development of pulmonary capillaries [19] so it is likely that the endothelium plays important roles in successful regeneration after injury. Our data from subjects with subclinical asymptomatic ILD suggest that expansion of bronchial populations happens early in the disease process (Figure 5), consistent with the possibility [105] that abnormal angiogenesis contributes to the dysfunctional tissue repair that is a hallmark of ILD. For proper wound healing across tissues, granulation tissue develops with significant angiogenesis of fenestrated vessels carrying cells and nutrients into areas enriched in connective tissue produced by activated fibroblasts. Appropriate regeneration concludes with regression of granulation tissue and restoration of normal architecture with return of tissue‐specific niches and cells [106, 107]. Intriguingly, the expanded bronchial vessels in ILD have similar morphology [108] to those observed in granulation tissue, which is also characterized by collagen‐rich fibrotic stroma, fibroblast activation, and vascular leak. However, regeneration fails to occur in progressive pulmonary fibrosis, with alveoli replaced by areas of scar containing COL15A1+ vessels rather than lung‐specific vasculature. In ILD, expansion of bronchial vessels with alveolar capillary dropout mirrors the epithelial shift from alveolar to airway phenotypes. The presence of these COL15A1+ vessels may represent an integrative measure between the degree of ongoing lung damage and rate of functional regeneration and given their early appearance, have the potential to influence disease progression.

Modeling the role of a systemic bronchial circulation in disease progression is limited with current murine models of lung fibrosis. Mice, unlike rats, lack subcarinal arteries and a systemic bronchial circulation [109]; accordingly, in response to pulmonary artery ligation, neovessels arise primarily from the parietal pleura fed from intercostal arteries. We and others [110, 111] suggest that vascular parameters (e.g. perfusion, permeability) measured in mouse models of lung fibrosis and cancer should consider whether the vessel type under investigation mirrors the relevant vessel subtype(s) in human disease. While features of alveolar capillaries appear conserved between mouse and human [15, 17], the architecture of systemic vessels in the lungs is dissimilar [110, 112, 113]. Murine alveolar capillaries do not appear to readily transform into systemic bronchial vasculature in the setting of injury, suggesting that either the increase in human COL15A1+ bronchial vasculature is driven more by angiogenesis than transformation or murine capillaries do not retain the transformational capabilities of human capillaries. Expansion of fibrotic lung modeling into animals with bronchial circulations [114] can yield insights into the role of the bronchial circulation in the pathogenesis of ILD.

While genetic evidence points towards epithelium as an inciting cell type in fibrogenesis, disease progression likely requires an integrated injury response involving multiple cell types that makeup the distal lung parenchyma. Here, we provide additional support to a limited number of studies [4, 40, 41, 103] that have shown expansion of an ectopic population of endothelial cells in the fibrotic lung that currently have an unknown role in disease progression. Notably, early fibrosis in IPF occurs in subpleural regions [115, 116] that contain bronchial ECs, indicating an anatomical correlation between fibrogenesis and bronchial ECs. Future studies that employ appropriate model systems are needed to determine causal relationships between these associations and disease pathogenesis. Integration of rigorous clinical phenotyping with mechanistic studies will contribute to our collective goal of developing effective anti‐fibrotic therapeutic strategies.

sec.title: Semi‐Supervised Clustering of All Cells
sec.p: scRNA‐seq data from VUMC/TGen (GSE135893) [8], Yale/BWH (GSE136831) [4], Pittsburgh (GSE128033) [117], and Northwestern (GSE122960) [9] were downloaded as a single Seurat (v4.0.6) [118] object from Bui et al. [51] (Banovich lab) (https://github.com/tgen/banovichlab/tree/master/Disease_lung_COVID19_2020) [51]. Human data from GSE128169 [10] and GSE132771 (unsorted “All cells” samples) [12] were also downloaded and converted to Seurat objects, then each data set was filtered using the code: subset(< seurat_object > , subset = nCount_RNA > = 1000 & nFeature_RNA > 999 & nFeature_RNA < 8000 & percent. mt < 25). The six datasets were merged, split into a list of six objects according to study accession using ‘SplitObject’, then integrated using the functions ‘SelectIntegrationFeatures’ (nfeatures = 5000, fvf. nfeatures = 5000), ‘FindIntegrationAnchors’ (reduction = “rpca”, anchor. features = features, n. trees = 55, max. features = 250), and ‘IntegrateData’. Samples with greater than 500 cells were carried forward for downstream analyses. Semi‐supervised clustering was performed using SCINA [119] (https://github.com/jcao89757/SCINA) with default parameters, rm_overlap = FALSE, allow_unknown = FALSE, and reference signatures were informed by markers from [4] and [15] (Supplemental Table S1). To identify endothelial cells as a broad cluster, ‘FindClusters’ (resolution = 0.008) was applied to the integrated Seurat object. Endothelial cells were subsetted and re‐clustered using the ‘FindClusters’ workflow (resolution = 0.3). For each donor sample, the proportional makeup of each cell type (Figure 1B) was computed using propeller within the ‘speckle’ R package [52], and significance was determined by t‐test followed by multiple testing correction using Benjamini‐Hochberg False Discovery Rate.

sec.title: Integration of Endothelial Cells from Multiple Datasets
sec.p: The Seurat object from Bui et al. [51] with associated cell‐level metadata was downloaded from https://github.com/tgen/banovichlab/tree/master/Disease_lung_COVID19_2020, containing samples from VUMC/TGen Yale/BWH, Northwestern, and Pittsburgh (Figure S6); only cells annotated as “endothelial” were carried forward for downstream analysis. For the two smaller datasets that lacked cell‐level metadata (GSE128169 [10, 12] and GSE132771 [12]), only cells that clustered with ECs from Bui et al. were carried forward for downstream analysis (Figure S6).

Batch‐corrected normalized data from NSCLC samples [50] were downloaded from https://endotheliomics.shinyapps.io/lung_ectax/. From this data set, we selected cells annotated as “arteries”, “postcapillary”, “activated pcv”, “immature”, “tip cell”, “alveolar type I”, and “alveolar type II” for integration with ECs from the ILD studies discussed above.

ECs from the seven datasets were integrated and clustered by an unsupervised approach using the Seurat ‘IntegrateData’ and ‘FindClusters’ (resolution = 0.4) workflows. This integrated endothelial cell data set is accessible for further exploration for non‐bioinformaticians using an interactive webtool at https://eengelbrecht.shinyapps.io/ILD_NSCLC_ECs/ [120].

Differential gene expression was evaluated between groups of cells using the “wilcoxauc” function of the R package presto [121] (https://github.com/immunogenomics/presto) using the code: wilcoxauc(< seurat_object >, ‘cluster’, seurat_assay = ‘RNA’, assay = ‘data’) (Supplemental Table S4). Cell‐level metadata for the integrated EC seurat object are available in Supplemental Table S5.

Expression plots, as well as boxplots and stacked bar plots of cell proportions, were generated using the R package dittoSeq [122]. Seurat, ggplot2 (v3.4.4), and our interactive ShinyApp (https://eengelbrecht.shinyapps.io/ILD_NSCLC_ECs/).

sec.title: Immunofluorescent Staining
sec.p: Tissues underwent deparaffinization followed by antigen retrieval with either citrate pH 6 or TE pH 9 using a pressure cooker. Slides were washed and permeabilized with PBS containing 0.1% Triton‐X100 (wash/perm solution solution). Block‐stain solution (PBS with 1% BSA and 0.3% Triton‐X100 was used to block slides for 1 h before staining as well as dilute antibodies. All primary antibody staining was performed overnight at 4 C. The following primary antibodies were used: COL15A1 (Sigma# HPA017913, 1:200), COL15A1 (R&D#NBP2‐46325 OTI1C5, 1:50) ACKR1 (ThermoFisher #PA5‐82549, 1:50), PGF (Proteintech# 10642‐1‐AP, 1:400), ERG (Abcam #ab214341 EPR3864, 1:100), CD31 (Abcam # ab9498, JC/70 A, 1:100). Following primary antibody staining, slides were washed and incubated with Hoechst (Life Technologies # H3570, 1:2000) and compatible secondaries diluted to 1:400 (Life Technologies’ Alexa Fluor series 488, 594, and 647) for 2 h at room temperature. Specimens were then washed and coverslips mounted.

sec.title: Immunohistochemistry Staining and Quantification
sec.p: Trichrome and H&E staining were performed by the MGH pathology core. IHC staining for COL15A1 (Sigma# HPA017913) was optimized by and performed by the MGH pathology core using the Ventana Discovery Ultra system with “CC2” (sodium citrate‐based) antigen retrieval, primary antibody dilution of 1:500, and Diaminobenzidine (DAB) as the chromogen.

Positive staining for COL15A1 on samples from the early, asymptomatic cohort biopsies was quantified by manually counting positive vascular structures appearing outside of typical locations (> 100 um away from either airway or pleural structures). An entire slide from each subject was tilescanned into a single image and then scored. The number of vessels was then normalized to the size of tissue on the slide as measured in mm2.

For explanted tissues, automated quantification was used given that the IPF/SSc tissues contained too much staining to feasibly count manually. The entire slide was tilescanned as a single image, and the DAB channel was extracted from the image using a threshold to classify positive staining vessels. The “analyze particles” function from FIJI was used to measure the percentage of area staining positive and to report the number of positive staining vessels. The fraction of the imaged slide area occupied by the tissue was measured and used to normalize the percent slide area staining positive.

sec.title: Microscopy and Imaging
sec.p: Immunofluorescent staining was imaged using a Zeiss Axioimager M2 upright fluorescent microscope. IHC and Trichrome images were obtained used an Axio scan Z1 slide scanning system.
